Mice slept 70% less after scientists switched off these brain cells

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (879 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Why does being awake for too long make us increasingly desperate for sleep?
  • Sources indicate that the longer we go without sleep, the more difficult it becomes to stay awake.
  • Researchers led by Professor Alex Schier at the Biozentrum, University of Basel, have now identified brain cells that help regulate this process.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Why does being awake for too long make us increasingly desperate for sleep? Scientists at the University of Basel in Switzerland have identified two groups of brain cells in mice that become more active the longer the animals remain awake. These neurons play a critical role in creating the pressure to sleep, offering upcoming clues about how the brain regulates our need for rest.

Sources indicate that the longer we go without sleep, the more difficult it becomes to stay awake. This buildup of sleep pressure, often called sleep drive, helps ensure that extended periods of wakefulness are followed by longer and deeper sleep. Although sleep is essential for survival, exactly how the brain measures time spent awake and converts that information into an increasing need for sleep has remained a mystery.

Researchers led by Professor Alex Schier at the Biozentrum, University of Basel, have now identified brain cells that help regulate this process. The work was conducted in collaboration with scientists from Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Auburn University.

"We have identified neuronal populations that monitor prolonged wakefulness and actively promote sleep," indicates Alex Schier. "This is an vital missing piece of the puzzle in understanding why we become sleepy.".

Scientists Identify Brain Cells That Drive Sleep Pressure.

According to recent reports, to investigate how sleep pressure develops, the team studied patterns of brain activity in mice under three different conditions: normal cycles of sleeping and waking, extended sleep deprivation, and recovery sleep. By comparing these patterns, they identified brain regions whose activity changed according to how long the animals had been awake.

Within one of these regions, the brainstem, researchers pinpointed two groups of neurons involved in controlling sleep drive. Known as GABAergic and serotonergic neurons, both groups became progressively more active as the mice remained awake. Their activity then decreased once the animals fell asleep.

The next question was whether these neurons simply tracked how long the mice had been awake or actually helped create the growing need for sleep.

Industry observers note that experiments revealed that the neurons were directly involved in driving sleep. When researchers artificially activated both groups, the mice slept longer and more deeply, showing the same type of recovery sleep normally seen after extended wakefulness. When the neurons were inhibited, however, the animals slept substantially less and were able to remain awake and alert.

Recent findings suggest that "These neurons do not simply signal that an animal has been awake," says Schier. "Our experiments show that they are crucial to promote sleep, and that they may be key components of the neural circuitry that generates sleep drive.".

In a recent development, the results provide particularly strong evidence that certain neurons activated during wakefulness do more than register lost sleep. They actively help generate the pressure that eventually pushes the brain toward sleep.

Mice Sleep 70% Less When Key Neurons Are Inhibited.

Further experiments produced an especially surprising result. When scientists suppressed both groups of neurons for an extended period, the mice slept approximately 70% less than normal.

It has been revealed that even more unexpectedly, most of these animals did not display some of the serious behavioral problems typically associated with prolonged sleep deprivation. Despite getting dramatically less sleep, many avoided impairments that researchers would ordinarily expect.

These findings suggest that the identified neurons influence not only the amount of time animals spend sleeping, but also how strongly the pressure to sleep increases during wakefulness.

Rather than simply responding to exhaustion, the brain appears to use specific neural circuits to actively regulate the growing need for rest.

A Upcoming Direction for Sleep Research.

Sources indicate that understanding these circuits could open crucial latest avenues for studying sleep and its effects on the body. Researchers now hope to determine how the identified neurons communicate with other brain regions and what molecular processes allow them to generate sleep pressure.

"Future studies could reveal how these neurons interact with the rest of the brain, and how sleep drive is generated at the molecular level," claims Dr. William Joo, first author of the study. "Our ability to stably transform sleep behavior also allows us to explore adaptations to long-term sleep loss - this may eventually reveal ways to confer resilience to sleep deprivation and other physiological challenges.".

The findings establish that GABAergic and serotonergic neurons in the brainstem become increasingly active during prolonged wakefulness and play an essential role in promoting sleep.

Determining exactly how the brain makes sleep increasingly difficult to resist remains a major objective of sleep research. Beyond improving scientists' understanding of sleep disorders, this discovery could help explain how the nervous system adapts to extended wakefulness and other physical challenges.

Ultimately, a clearer understanding of the brain circuits responsible for sleep pressure could inspire new treatments and potentially reveal ways to improve resilience to sleep deprivation.

In a recent development, the Mortality’s Tenderness banner features five upcoming limited-time 5-Star Memories, one each for the game’s five love interests. When you reach Rank 1 for any new Memory from the banner, you’ll earn a Memory-themed outfit with a special colour that matches your chosen love interest.

Illusio returns as part of the new event, too, letting you customise the look of Kindled Moments across all five new Memories. #201102. America is building just 10% of the power lines it needs, experts warn

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1172 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

America is building just 10% of the power lines it needs, experts warn

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1172 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that america's electricity needs are growing rapidly, but the nation's aging power grid is struggling to keep up.
  • In a Policy Forum paper published in Science, energy policy researchers from Carnegie Mellon University and the University of California San Diego warn that the United States faces one of the world's most serious bottlenecks in electricity transmission.
  • America Is Building Just 10% of the Power Lines It Needs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that america's electricity needs are growing rapidly, but the nation's aging power grid is struggling to keep up. More electric vehicles, increased electricity use in heavy industry, and the explosive growth of data centers are driving demand higher, putting additional pressure on an infrastructure system that is already falling behind.

In a Policy Forum paper published in Science, energy policy researchers from Carnegie Mellon University and the University of California San Diego warn that the United States faces one of the world's most serious bottlenecks in electricity transmission. The problem could have major consequences for electricity prices, grid reliability, and the nation's economic future.

America Is Building Just 10% of the Power Lines It Needs.

In a recent development, A major concern is the extremely slow pace of transmission construction. Over the past five years, the continental United States has added an average of only about 500 miles of high-voltage transmission lines annually. Research suggests the country needs approximately 5,000 miles each year to triple the size of its interregional transmission network by 2050 and accommodate future electricity demand.

That means the U.S. is building newly introduced high-voltage transmission lines at just one-tenth of the estimated pace needed.

Sources indicate that high-voltage transmission lines serve as the highways of the electricity system, carrying large amounts of power over long distances from generating facilities to communities and businesses. Connecting regional grids allows electricity to flow more easily between areas, helping balance supply and demand when local power production falls short.

In a recent development, studies have shown that larger, better-connected electricity networks can reduce costs for consumers while also lowering the risk of catastrophic blackouts. When one region experiences a power shortage, electricity from another region can help keep the lights on.

Despite these advantages, expanding the nation's transmission infrastructure has proved extraordinarily difficult.

The Biggest Obstacle Isn't Technology.

According to the researchers (Madeline Yozwiak, David G. Victor, and M. Granger Morgan), the main barriers to modernizing America's power grid are political and regulatory rather than technological.

Sources indicate that responsibility for approving major transmission projects is divided among federal agencies, state governments, local authorities, and private companies. Each has its own priorities and interests, creating numerous opportunities for proposed power lines to be delayed or blocked.

Existing electric utilities can also have financial reasons to resist stronger connections between regions. Greater competition from electricity suppliers elsewhere could weaken their influence over local markets, reducing the incentive to support projects that would benefit the broader electricity system.

As a result, even transmission projects that could lower costs and improve reliability across the country can struggle to gain approval.

Three Ways to Fix America's Power Grid Crisis.

To address the growing shortfall, the researchers recommend a three-part strategy combining stronger government action, modern transmission technologies, international cooperation, and regulatory reform.

Sources indicate that 1. Make better use of existing federal powers and advanced technologies.

Recent findings suggest that the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) and the Department of Energy (DOE) already have legal authorities that could help move important transmission projects forward. The researchers argue that these agencies should use those powers more effectively, including identifying transmission corridors of national importance and addressing disputes that prevent projects from receiving state-level approval.

Sources indicate that technological improvements could also dramatically increase the amount of electricity the grid can carry. One approach, known as reconductoring, involves replacing existing power line conductors with more advanced materials capable of transmitting more electricity without necessarily requiring entirely newly introduced routes.

Other advances, including newer High-Voltage Direct Current (VSC-HVDC) systems, offer additional ways to move large amounts of electricity efficiently. The researchers suggest that modern transmission technologies could double or even triple capacity.

It has been revealed that underground high-voltage direct current (HVDC) cables offer another promising option. These systems can carry substantial amounts of electricity over long distances and could potentially be installed along existing highways and railroad corridors. Using these established routes could help avoid some of the land-use disputes and approval challenges that often delay conventional transmission projects.

2. Learn from countries that have already overcome similar obstacles.

The United States trails several international counterparts in building long-distance HVDC infrastructure and coordinating electricity transmission across regional and national boundaries.

According to recent reports, other countries have demonstrated that large transmission projects can move forward despite complicated political approval processes. Some have also successfully deployed underground HVDC systems on a large scale.

Industry observers note that rather than developing every solution independently, the researchers suggest that the U.S. should study these international experiences and adapt approaches that have already proved successful.

One proposal is to establish an international forum involving electricity regulators and other experts, potentially led by organizations such as the National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners (NARUC). Such a forum could help American policymakers identify effective regulatory practices, planning strategies, and technologies used elsewhere.

3. Create a national commission to break the political deadlock.

The researchers also recommend establishing a Presidential-Congressional Transmission Commission to address the political and regulatory conflicts that have slowed grid expansion for decades.

Modeled on previous successful bipartisan commissions, the proposed group would bring together key stakeholders to negotiate difficult decisions and develop a coordinated plan for reform.

Its responsibilities would include recommending changes to state and federal laws, examining whether FERC should receive broader authority over the locations of upcoming transmission projects, and developing financial incentives for companies that lead new construction.

The commission could also recommend financial rewards for communities that host transmission infrastructure, helping ensure that local residents share in the benefits of projects that serve larger regions.

Why America's Power Grid Crisis Could Get Worse.

Industry observers note that the researchers emphasize that the underlying challenge is not a lack of engineering solutions. Instead, the country's divided decision-making system allows individual stakeholders to obstruct projects that could deliver substantial nationwide benefits.

It has been revealed that "The fundamental challenge isn't technical, it's jurisdictional. Authority is divided among federal, state, and private entities, each with distinct priorities. When every stakeholder possesses the power to say no, even high-value projects that benefit the entire nation struggle to move forward," the authors warn.

Their assessment suggests that simply continuing with the existing system of overlapping regulations and fragmented authority will not be enough to meet America's growing electricity needs.

Without meaningful changes to how transmission projects are planned, approved, and built, the United States risks a prolonged infrastructure shortfall. The researchers warn that failing to resolve these problems could weaken electricity reliability and inflict lasting damage on the national economy, even as demand for power continues to climb.

Tested: 1979 Buick Century Turbo Coupe Is a Rolling Contradiction

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2354 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Caranddriver

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A paradox, according to a well­-thumbed copy of Webster’s Fresh World, is a statement that seems contradictory, but may be true.
  • On the other hand we have this Tur­bo Coupe posturing about in its rackish, spoilered finery, squatting on its we­-mean-business fat tires, its twin pipes burbling, acting more Trans Am than Buick.
  • Buick started making out-of-character performance noises a few years ago when its chief engineer, Lloyd Reuss, and a band of enthusiastic young engi­neers decided to crank up a turbocharg­ing project for the V-6 engine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From the June 1979 glitch of Car and Driver.

It has been revealed that A paradox, according to a well­-thumbed copy of Webster’s Fresh World, is a statement that seems contradictory, but may be true. Which brings us imme­diately to the Buick Century Turbo Coupe. On one hand it most definitely is a Buick, which is automatically a state­ment. As most of us were growing up, the Buicks in our lives belonged to the family doctor or other such community pillars. Buicks were sedate, relatively ex­pensive cars—stop-offs on the way up the GM ladder for the man with the growing bank account, or the highest reasonable aspirations for the workaday man who longed to rise out of Ford and Chevy land.

On the other hand we have this Tur­bo Coupe posturing about in its rackish, spoilered finery, squatting on its we­-mean-business fat tires, its twin pipes burbling, acting more Trans Am than Buick. A contradiction.

Buick started making out-of-character performance noises a few years ago when its chief engineer, Lloyd Reuss, and a band of enthusiastic young engi­neers decided to crank up a turbocharg­ing project for the V-6 engine. Their ef­forts were first seen in the 1975 Indy pace car, which also sported some very un-Buick-like suspension. In 1977 Buick offered a slick Sport Coupe variation on the LeSabre and Regal theme. The Le­Sabre version we tested was so good it elicited comments like “a breath of fresh air for people who’ve hungered to own a good-handling American car.” And one exuberant staffer mentioned all it needed was a three-pointed star on the hood to make it a Mercedes-class piece. In 1978 the turbo motor went into pro­duction, and the stage was set for this year's Turbo Coupe.

See all results for used cars for sale near 98012.

Bruce Robinson is a project engineer at Buick’s Flint, Michigan, headquar­ters, and one of those enthusiastic types Reuss brought in to spice up Buick’s slide-rule department. Reuss is gone now—he’s chief engineer over at Chev­rolet—but Robinson and the Reuss en­thusiasm still exist. Robinson was as­signed the Turbo Coupe. He didn’t build it single-handedly, but as much as any car that pops off the line can be said to be one man’s baby, the Turbo Coupe is his.

Sources indicate that “We wanted to go from GT, like the LeSabre and Regal Sport Coupes, to All Out,” Robinson explains. “We wanted to make it go, and handle, and stop like no other Buick.”.

He did it, he explains, by creating what Buick now calls the FE1 package, a giant step up from the existing FE2, which is Buick’s equivalent of Chevro­let’s famous F41 handling upgrade. The FE1, available only on the Turbo Coupe, is basically stiffer springs, steer­ing changes, and wider wheels. The front spring rates have been increased from the regular Sport Coupe specs of 365 pounds per inch to a giganto 440. Rear springs are up to 140 lbs/in from 125. (For further comparison, the base V-6 Century coupe has spring rates, front/rear, of 300/115.) Anti-roll bars are the same for FE1 and FE2: 32 mm front, 22 mm rear; but another major up­grade for the Turbo came in the rear upper-control-arm bushings, little de­vices we don’t think much about but which have a lot to do with transient re­sponse. The base and Sport Coupe ver­sions have bushings rated at 20,000 lbs/in; the Turbo Coupe is fitted with 35,000-lbs/in bushings. Rounding out the FE2 package is a quicker steering ra­tio, 14:1 instead of 15.13:1, and P205/70R-14 radials on seven-inch rims.

See all results for used cars for sale near 98012.

According to recent reports, but as much as we wanted to know all that good spring and tire stuff, we were even more curious about the exhaust system. It is, in a word, loud. We spent a lot of time playing with the throttle and letting off in low and second just to hear that sound-from-the-past, that Golden Oldie exhaust noise. How'd Robinson do it?

It has been revealed that the sound, he reveals, was a specifi­cally planned part of the overall image. They got it by the simple expedient of routing the exhaust into a single con­verter and then out into a pair of ex­haust pipes that carry a resonator each. No mufflers.

“A delightful byproduct,” Robinson gleefully reveals, “was an extra ten horsepower due to the reduced back pressure.” The odds on finding ten horsepower these days without spend­ing ’leventeen trillion dollars in devel­opment are about the same as Bianca and her pals dropping by your place for dinner tonight: slim to none.

In a recent development, that throaty exhaust note, by the way, is more evident inside the Turbo Coupe than outside. The body acts as a sound chamber to increase the effect. “The noise level passed the EPA tests,” Robinson indicates, “but we’re not about to ask them to check it again to make sure.” Right.

So Robinson and his associates have built a Buick with all the right suspen­sion bits and pieces, they’ve come up with a creditable 175 horses to move it around, they’ve given it an exhaust sys­tem to warm the cockles of an old hot rodder’s heart, and they’ve dressed it up with spoilers and flat-black paint. Why, we had to wonder, after doing all that, did they leave out some traditional, mandatory even, performance-car parts, like a manual transmission and an in­strument panel with some gauges?

It has been revealed that “Simple,” Robinson claims. “Money.”.

Recent findings suggest that adding a manual transmission would have required a complete 50,000-mile EPA durability test, and that costs hun­dreds of thousands. Ditto a different in­strument panel. Buick didn’t have any­thing on the shelf that would have bolt­ed in. Designing a new panel and tool­ing up to produce it would also have cost hundreds of thousands.

Industry observers note that “Anything you spend on building a latest model, or a new version of an exist­ing car,” Robinson explains, “you have to figure you can recover in sales.” And Buick doesn’t figure to sell too many Turbo Coupes, it turns out. It's an image car, a showroom-traffic build­er, so if you see one on the floor of your local Buick dealer, you’re probably looking at his allotment for the year. Should you jump at it?

Sources indicate that the Turbo Coupe is easily the best-­looking of all the “aero” designs, which Buick and Olds offer in two- and four­-door versions. The improvement in looks seems to come from the simple addition of the rear-deck spoiler, which also happens to reduce overall drag, Buick reports, by a healthy 18 percent. (The two-door aero design, by the way, will be around at least through 1980; the ugly four-door is going away.).

Inside, as we’ve hinted, there is little to distinguish the Turbo Coupe from its lesser brethren. The handsome, but un­informative, instrument panel contains a tricolor turbo-boost indicator that reads out in one, A Little, and Whoosh. Our test car had vinyl buckets, and while they provide pretty good sup­port in all the right places, they are as slick as greased owl potty. Cloth is avail­able, however, and we recommend it.

Sources indicate that over the road, the Turbo’s yes-I-am, no-I’m-not nature surfaces again. De­spite all the good things Robinson and his merry band have wrought, the car’s manners are still rather Buick-like. Which isn’t necessarily all bad. Your teeth aren’t jarred by every tar strip, and the car is very quiet at cruise. But there is an unexpected numbness in the steering that should have been factored out. Response is good, but that all-crucial feel is missing.

In a recent development, despite the suspension modifications, the Turbo Coupe is still an understeer­er. That’s to be expected, so no points lost there. General Motors is a firm be­liever that understeer is safer than over­steer. Better, the reasoning goes, the in­competents plow off the road nose-first, scrubbing speed all the way, than have the tail leading the procession at prodi­gious speed. Fair enough, because the knowledgeable Trans Am or Z28 driver can put the boot into his mount at the proper time and induce some very pleasant oversteer. Not so with the Tur­bo Coupe; the little engine-that-would­-be-a-V-8 just doesn’t produce enough torque swiftly enough to let you play the tail-out game with much success. The boost gauge may be up there in Whoosh, but the tail will be dutifully following the furrow the front end is plowing. We’re talking about out there at the cop-baiting, wife-scaring, dog­-cowering limit, of course. In normal brisk motoring, the suspension does a good job. There’s no willow-wallow here, thank you.

Recent findings suggest that the Coupe also does other good things. You’ll note that our comparison graphs show it at the top in acceleration ­and braking. Straight-line numbers will not disappoint.

In a recent development, the Turbo Coupe certainly has the flash and dash Buick wants for its show­rooms, and it’s sure to draw its share of peekers and pokers and hood lifters. The traditional Buick buyer will peek and poke and then head off to the Elec­tra or LeSabre four-doors. The curious that stopped off on their way to price Trans Am and Z28s will poke and peek with a good bit more interest. And when they learn they can have a bare-bones Turbo Coupe for a little more than $6000, they may even give it some seri­ous thought. But our best guess is they’ll eventually find their way back to those other showrooms. The Turbo Coupe, as good a Buick as it is, doesn’t seem to be right for either group.

What we want is Bruce Robinson and his boys to turn their attention to a new Skylark Sport Coupe. Turbo that little honey, slap the FE1 package on it, and stand back. When we suggested that to Robinson, his eyes lit up with what could only be engineer-type lust. So maybe it’ll happen. And maybe it’ll even have a tachometer.

It has been revealed that I must admit, the first night I drove the Turbo Coupe I kept putting my foot into it and running up through the gears, then backing off and doing it again and again, all the way home. The pumped-up little six, all snarling and willing, was just too inviting for me to ignore. Sometimes I’d even drop it into low and back off just to listen to the popping of the exhaust as it simmered down. I acted as silly as a newly licensed adolescent that night, but you just can’t resist playing in the Turbo Coupe. It’s that kind of car.

But what turned me on the most was the message hidden within its sophisticat­ed mechanicals: a new generation of mus­cle cars, one that pays its respects to both ecology and our tight petroleum supply, is not only possible, it’s just around the corner. All Buick has to do is work its tur­bocharging wizardry on the half-ton-­lighter Skylark front-driver and we’ll have the first of that new breed. Let us pray. —Rich Ceppos.

In a recent development, I happen to be a firm believer in turbo­charging and all the wonderful things it can do for our cars—David E. Davis, Jr., to the contrary—but this Turbo Coupe from Buick stretches the very heartstrings of my enthusiasm. Past the limit. It’s a horrible fate for any engine as spunky as Buick’s turbo V-6. This motor should be zapping around a 2000-pound sports car or burning the tires off Buick’s chic little Skyhawk. Instead, it’s sentenced to the homeliest hunchback sedan Buick has stamped out in recent history. Grown men wince at the sight of this TR7 garage on wheels. And I wince at the thought of such an eager engine straining its heart out against a 3500-pound curb weight and an automatic transmission, without so much as a tachometer or a boost gauge to register the effort. To finish off the in­sult, this Century’s all gussied up in what I assume is Buick’s idea of a performance disguise. It looks like something the local sheriff would use to sneak up on the kids down at Shakey's. They wouldn’t be con­vinced, and neither am I. —Don Sherman.

Normally, when you dip the accelerator on a six-cylinder American car, it gives you the feeling you’re saving gas. Saving gas is a noble pastime but the feeling of saving gas is drudgery, right up there with Cometing out the sink.

That is why I think this Buick stands to give the American six-cylinder a good name. When you dip the pedal, things hap­pen. First off, the whole dashboard glows orange. (Knepper noted the illumination comes from the boost light, but it’s hidden behind so many spokes and switches that I never actually saw it.) Then the exhaust turns mean and the bucket seat gets all pushy. Instead of saving gas, you get the feeling you’re hurrying.

Really, except for a count of the spark-­plug wires, there’s nothing six-cylinder about this car. It feels more like a high schooler’s hot rod, glass packs and all, and I had the urge to head on down to the drive-in and burn some rubber. I haven’t been in that mood for years. —Patrick Bedard.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that there is a lot that you can do in the first chapter of Grand Theft Auto 6.
  • After chapter one, everything in GTA 6 changes, and you don’t have the opportunity to get everything done that you might want to, so you want to be sure that you have a checklist and that you complete it before making your way to Vice City and starting bigger and better things.
  • Industry observers note that note: It is vital to note that taking up Mattia’s offer will end the first chapter of the game.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that there is a lot that you can do in the first chapter of Grand Theft Auto 6. You can deep sea dive for treasure, hang out with friends, complete missions, set up for Lucia, and a lot more. However, some of this absolutely needs to be done before you hit the end of the first chapter.

After chapter one, everything in GTA 6 changes, and you don’t have the opportunity to get everything done that you might want to, so you want to be sure that you have a checklist and that you complete it before making your way to Vice City and starting bigger and better things.

Industry observers note that note: It is vital to note that taking up Mattia’s offer will end the first chapter of the game. There will also be spoilers ahead about chapter one.

It has been revealed that jason and Lucia have a chance to be madly in love in the beginning of the game. If you prepare for Lucia to get out of prison, work on Jason’s appearance, and focus on how they interact with each other, it will build a solid foundation.

It has been revealed that there is a hard reset that comes at the end of the first chapter, and for a while, Lucia will be on her own while Jason recovers. With that being said, it will take a bit of a toll on their relationship.

This means that if you raise it up very high in the beginning, you won’t need to worry about needing to rebuild it as much later in the game, saving you a bit of time later on.

Immediately after setting up your BuckMe account, you are told that you need to start saving money. The first goal in the game is to have a total savings of $5,000 stashed away. This is a pretty easy goal to hit, especially since there are a fair number of money-making opportunities in the first chapter.

You want to make sure that you hit this goal, as when the hard reset comes at the end of the chapter, you will lose everything except what is in your savings account.

As an added bonus, putting money away into your savings account will also raise your relationship, so it is a win-win situation. After you have everything saved up, the rest of your money is stuff you can play with.

Now that you have saved up the necessary cash for your family savings account, you might have some money burning a hole in your pocket. It is time to go on a bit of a shopping spree.

Recent findings suggest that as I remarked, you won’t be able to take this money with you into chapter two, so you will want to spend all of it. Buy some clothes, and definitely upgrade your weapons.

Recent findings suggest that there is no point in upgrading your car, as you will lose this after chapter one. Instead, focus on increasing your wardrobe and upgrading your weapons as these will carry over into the next chapter.

There are some missions that you only have access to in the first chapter, and some of them belong to Shirley - Jason’s neighbor. She is a kind lady, and she will occasionally ask you to complete a few tasks.

These consist of getting her some alcohol, and stealing a mobility scooter from a lady nearby. They are fun short missions that you can complete within a few minutes, but they are worth doing because they are quite fun.

Don’t worry about the treasure hunting, as you will be able to come back to it later on. Only certain missions disappear after the first chapter.

Recent findings suggest that there’s tons of details in GTA 6, which means that there are a bunch of collectibles that you can find scattered about. Some of these collectibles are books and magazines, and several of them are found around Jason’s house.

Before you end chapter one, you will want to get the books around Jason’s house. These include one in the bedroom, two in the living room, a magazine on the back deck, and one in the shed. Each of these disappears after the first chapter.

Along with this, you will want to grab the sunglasses in Donny’s trailer. You will make your way over there during one of the missions in the first chapter, so you shouldn’t miss out on them, but make sure to pick them up while you have the chance.

If you have been focused on upgrading your weapons, gathering clothes, and putting money into your savings, then you will probably need some extra cash in the first chapter. Instead of searching for treasure, you should instead focus on completing the lost drug missions.

There are four lost drug missions around Key Lento and up to the Grassrivers. These are special missions that end up disappearing after chapter one ends, so you will not have the ability to go back and complete them later on.

Since this is the only time you have access to them, you may as well complete them for the extra cash and spend it on stuff that will help you later in the game.

Recent findings suggest that while I have already established that buying weapons is important because they carry over, it is also important to grab the unique weapons that are obtainable early in the game. There are a couple weapons that you can find around the islands in Key Lento, and they will carry you in later parts of the game.

For instance, the Assassin Pistol can be found on a small dinghy on an island and it is great for completing missions stealthily in later parts of the game, and it has become one of my go-to weapons for staying hidden.

Industry observers note that there is also a shotgun that you can find that is quite powerful. It gets outclassed by other unique weapons later on, but it is great to have in chapter two.

In a recent development, one thing that is nice about GTA 6 is that it gives you the option to manually save. This means that you can create save points at key points in the game so that you can return to them later on.

I highly recommend completing what you can in chapter one and then creating a save point right before you go to do the tourist trap mission, as this is the last mission of the chapter, and it is also the point of no return.

If you want to play the game over but don’t want to deal with the slower pacing of the first chapter, you can skip all of that with a save right before the chapter change.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It seems that nowadays creature-collecting has become more popular than ever, no doubt helped by the likes of Palworld really blowing the doors off the concept after Pokémon dominated it for so long. And one of the cutest, lightweight takes has now hit pre-registration on mobile with World of Slime!

Industry observers note that world of Slime is, well, exactly as described. This cute top-down MMORPG is best described as a mix of Roco Kingdom with a RuneScape perspective, where you explore a world completing quests and tasks, while capturing cute slime creatures to join your roster.

There's also more straightforward MMORPG combat as you battle it out with huge bosses that stand in your way. It's not exactly World of Warcraft, but World of Slime undoubtedly has plenty in the way of potential. And that small scale makes it a perfect fit for mobile, alongside its adorable cast!

Industry observers note that at the same time, it's not been received without controversy, and presently sits at a mixed reception on Steam. Hopefully, that lacklustre reception doesn't translate to a lacking mobile launch. But if you are interested, you can pre-register for World of Slime now on the official site!

#201095. A simple metal is hiding a strange new form of magnetism

A simple metal is hiding a strange new form of magnetism

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1578 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A surprisingly simple metal has revealed an unusual form of magnetism that could open upcoming possibilities for quantum technology.
  • In a recent development, the material, known as europium silicide (EuSi), contains an intricate magnetic structure that influences how electrons move and how their spins are oriented.
  • The discovery is particularly significant because EuSi is a relatively simple metallic compound.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A surprisingly simple metal has revealed an unusual form of magnetism that could open upcoming possibilities for quantum technology. Researchers have found compelling evidence of a rare magnetic state in which electrons behave in unexpected ways, even though the material produces no overall magnetization.

In a recent development, the material, known as europium silicide (EuSi), contains an intricate magnetic structure that influences how electrons move and how their spins are oriented. This behavior is associated with a phenomenon called p-wave magnetism, an emerging area of research that could eventually help scientists develop newly introduced approaches to controlling electronic properties.

The discovery is particularly significant because EuSi is a relatively simple metallic compound. Unlike many materials previously considered for studying this exotic form of magnetism, it offers researchers a practical way to investigate the underlying physics in detail.

An Unexpected Discovery in a Simple Metal.

According to recent reports, the research began about three years ago at the Max Planck Institute for Chemical Physics of Solids (MPI CPfS) in Dresden, Germany. Dr. Erjian Cheng successfully grew high-quality single crystals of EuSi, providing the material needed for detailed experiments.

When researchers first examined the crystals using photoemission techniques, which probe the energies and behavior of electrons inside materials, they noticed something unexpected. The magnetic arrangement of the atoms had a remarkably strong influence on the electronic band structure, which describes the energy levels electrons can occupy and helps determine how a material conducts electricity.

It has been revealed that that observation raised an intriguing possibility. Could this simple compound contain an unconventional form of magnetism in which the spin of an electron is connected to the direction it travels?

"When we first measured the electronic structure of EuSi, we were surprised by the exceptionally large effect of magnetism on the electrons," explains Cheng. "That observation led us to investigate whether this simple compound could host a much more unusual magnetic state. The combination of crystal growth, neutron scattering and spin-resolved spectroscopy now provides compelling evidence for p-wave magnetism.".

In a recent development, answering that question required an international collaboration involving 38 scientists from 19 institutions. Participants included researchers from ShanghaiTech University, the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, the Max Planck Institute for the Physics of Complex Systems and Oak Ridge National Laboratory.

A Strange Form of Magnetism That Cancels Itself Out.

Industry observers note that ordinary magnets, such as those attached to refrigerators, typically rely on a magnetic arrangement called ferromagnetism. In these materials, many electron spins align in the same direction, producing an overall magnetic field.

At temperatures between approximately 33 and 62 kelvin, the magnetic moments of its europium atoms organize themselves into a repeating spiral pattern. These temperatures correspond to roughly minus 400 to minus 348 degrees Fahrenheit.

Sources indicate that each europium atom has a substantial magnetic moment, but their orientations balance one another across the spiral. As a result, the material has no net magnetization in this magnetic phase.

In a recent development, however, the absence of overall magnetization does not mean magnetism has stopped influencing the electrons. In fact, the researchers found that the spiral arrangement produces a highly unusual electronic structure.

In the proposed p-wave magnetic state, electrons traveling in opposite directions have opposite spin polarizations. Electron spin is a quantum property that gives electrons magnetic characteristics, although it should not be understood as an electron literally spinning like a tiny ball.

The relationship between an electron's direction of motion and its spin is called an odd-parity spin texture. This means that reversing the electron's momentum also reverses the associated spin polarization.

Other materials can display spin-dependent energy differences because of a phenomenon known as spin-orbit coupling, which connects an electron's motion to its spin. In EuSi, however, the unusual spin structure appears to arise mainly from interactions between magnetic moments and the specific symmetry of their spiral arrangement.

Experiments Reveal Evidence of Rare P-Wave Magnetism.

To determine whether EuSi truly exhibits the predicted magnetic state, the scientists combined several sophisticated experimental methods with theoretical calculations.

First, they used neutron diffraction, a technique that reveals how atoms and magnetic moments are arranged inside a material. These measurements confirmed that the europium magnetic moments form a spiral structure with the symmetry required for p-wave magnetism.

Sources indicate that next, the researchers examined the material using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy. This method measures the energies and momenta of electrons, allowing scientists to map the electronic structure.

The results showed that magnetic ordering substantially reorganizes the electron energy levels. In particular, the team observed magnetically driven energy separations exceeding 100 millielectronvolts, indicating an unusually strong influence of magnetism on electron behavior.

The most decisive evidence came from spin-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, which allowed the researchers to examine electron spin polarization directly.

It has been revealed that they observed that the sign of the spin polarization changed across successive magnetic Brillouin zones. These zones are regions of momentum space used by physicists to describe how electrons behave within a repeating magnetic structure.

The team also found that spin polarization became much weaker near locations where theoretical calculations predicted the p-wave spin texture should disappear.

Taken together, the measurements provide compelling experimental evidence consistent with the predicted p-wave magnetic state in EuSi.

A Hidden Magnetic Spiral With Two Different Orientations.

The researchers uncovered another unusual feature of EuSi involving chirality, a scientific term describing handedness.

A familiar example is the difference between a left hand and a right hand. They are mirror images, but they cannot be perfectly superimposed.

Something similar happens with the magnetic spiral inside EuSi. Although the underlying crystal has a centrosymmetric structure, meaning its atomic arrangement is unchanged by inversion through a central point, the magnetic spiral can twist in either of two opposite directions.

These different spiral orientations create magnetic regions, or domains, with opposite handedness.

Using magnetic force microscopy and spatially resolved photoemission spectroscopy, the scientists identified domains measuring approximately ten micrometers across. For perspective, ten micrometers is about one-tenth the thickness of a typical human hair.

When the researchers examined these regions using circularly polarized light, they detected different electronic responses depending on the handedness of the magnetic spiral.

This finding demonstrates that the direction in which the magnetic structure twists is linked to the material's electronic properties.

"What makes EuSi particularly exciting is that an unconventional electronic spin structure emerges from the magnetic order of a chemically simple metal," notes Prof. Claudia Felser, Director at MPI CPfS. "This demonstrates how the discovery of new materials can reveal entirely new electronic phenomena. EuSi now gives us an experimental platform to investigate how magnetic symmetry and chirality can be used to control electronic properties, with potential implications for future spintronics and unconventional superconductivity.".

Why This Discovery Matters for Quantum Technology.

One of the biggest challenges in studying p-wave magnetism has been finding materials that display the necessary magnetic properties while remaining practical for detailed experiments.

Earlier candidates have included insulating materials, as well as metals that develop the required magnetic order only at extremely low temperatures or have complicated symmetries that make their behavior difficult to interpret.

EuSi offers a particularly useful combination of characteristics.

It is a stoichiometric metal, meaning its constituent elements occur in a fixed chemical ratio. Researchers can also grow high-quality single crystals of the material, and its spiral magnetic arrangement has the symmetry associated with p-wave magnetism.

Together, these features make EuSi a promising experimental platform for exploring how exotic magnetic states influence the behavior of electrons.

Sources indicate that theoretical studies suggest that metallic p-wave magnets could display several remarkable properties. For example, they may allow electrons with particular spin orientations to carry electrical currents without requiring an external magnetic field.

They could also produce strong changes in spin polarization when an electric current is applied, potentially offering fresh ways to manipulate electronic behavior.

These possibilities are especially relevant to spintronics, a field of technology that seeks to use electron spin, rather than electrical charge alone, to process and store information.

Another intriguing possibility involves unconventional superconductivity, in which electrical current flows without resistance through superconducting states that differ from those found in conventional superconductors.

It has been revealed that importantly, these predicted effects have not yet been demonstrated in EuSi. The discovery does not establish that the material can already perform these functions, but it gives researchers a promising system in which to test the predictions.

More broadly, the findings highlight how much of a material's behavior can remain hidden beneath an apparently simple chemical composition.

Sources indicate that A solid's properties depend on more than the elements it contains or how its atoms are positioned. The arrangement of magnetic moments, the symmetries they create, and the quantum behavior of electrons can also produce entirely unexpected effects.

By revealing compelling evidence of p-wave magnetism in EuSi, researchers have gained a fresh opportunity to investigate these relationships and explore how unusual magnetic structures might eventually be used to control the electronic properties of future materials.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, ahead of the start of Battlefield 6’s Season 2 next week, Battlefield Studios has shared some insight into a few of the major goals the developer has with the Season 2 patch. The game’s second season was delayed in mid-January, and the developer even brought back Battlefield Labs to test out some of the newly introduced content and features coming with the new season.

Indeed, the broader goals BF Studios shared with players in a fresh blog post reflect some of what Labs players already went hands-on with, while others are the result of work on long-standing issues with both the game itself, as well as free-to-play mode Redsec.

We know that Season 2 is introducing a substantial upcoming map to the game, Contaminated, which the developer has been teasing. The map will indeed arrive in the first part of the season, and it’s going to do so alongside a new LTM that “introduces a new element of tactics.” A second, “high-intensity map” will debut later into the season, alongside another LTM where players battle through an underground base, in darkness.

Sources indicate that the real meat of the blog post, however, covers the broader gameplay changes everyone will see once the latest season kicks off. There’s a massive focus on player progression, especially when it concerns free-to-play Redsec players.

According to recent reports, challenges are being streamlined yet again, with more broad parameters that don’t require specific modes. Some, like dailies, will also allow for assists to count towards their criteria. Less restrictive challenges are welcome, but even more so is the faster battle pass progression.

BF Studios is changing the rate at which battle pass Tokens are earned from career XP, and making it so they’re earnable by playing the game normally, and by completing weekly challenges. These changes should also help Redsec players, who will also benefit from faster career and weapon XP earn rates - across both battle royale, and Gauntlet. In general, the career experience should feel more rewarding, especially for earlier ranks.

Weapon balance and recoil are two areas that will continue to evolve in Battlefield 6, it seems, and Season 2 is specifically tackling recoil patterns to make them more consistent when you compensate for them.

Sources indicate that movement is being adjusted with the Season 2 patch, too, though thankfully it’s limited to general feel that touches areas like vaulting, ladder transitions, and acceleration curves. You should also see better continuity and consistency between animations and feel.

It has been revealed that audio is getting a pass with the upcoming patch, especially when it comes to footstep and interaction audio. This also extends to something the developer has been working on improving for a while, and it has to do with how the game decides which audio tracks to prioritise in busy situations.

Tomorrow, the full Battlefield 6 Season 2 trailer will be released, while a more detailed roadmap is expected by the end of this week.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From the November/December 2026 issue of Car and Driver.

Industry observers note that more than double that if you count New Londons. There are about 30 Brightons, which I think means there are somewhere around 700 ways one could set up a London-to-Brighton antique-car run. Which, of course, is a totally normal thing to strategy, right?

Maybe a few of you with an interest in early automobiles recognize the combination of London and Brighton from the long-running English vintage-car meet that travels between those two cities every November. First run in 1896 by an intrepid group of early—very early—car enthusiasts, the Emancipation Run was held to mark one of the first increases in speed limits: from single digits (4 mph) to a downright scorching 14 mph.

The London-to-Brighton event, or, as it’s now known, the RM Sotheby’s London to Brighton Veteran Car Run, looks like fun, so we decided to have a go between our own London and Brighton in Michigan with some antique American cars.

See all results for used cars for sale near 19805.

Several things lined up well. Our course between London Township and the cute main street of Brighton was 57 miles, which is a good parallel to the U.K.’s 97-km (60-mile) route. Plenty of tree-lined country lanes connect the towns, a benefit when organizing a road trip for vehicles whose max speed may be more than 14 mph but still lags behind modern highway pace. Most vital, there’s a fantastic community of early-20th-century-car collectors in Michigan, so finding folks who were willing to take out their Fords, Oldsmobiles, Pullmans, and REOs was no problem.

What was a problem was finding a date. Every time I suggested a weekend, I’d get a flurry of texts and emails from the would-be participants. “So sorry,” stated Mark Turner. “There’s a steam-car rally that weekend.” It might have also been Turner who couldn’t do another date because of a meet for vintage Bentleys. “I don’t know if I could do June 6th because we have an HCCA [Horseless Carriage Club of America] tour down in Georgia,” said Brent Terry, with apologies. Eventually, I just picked something and hoped a few of the crew would manage to fit it into their busy, brassy schedules.

An 1865 regulation required a flagger with a red warning cloth to walk ahead of any roadgoing mechanical vehicles and limited their max speed to just 4 mph on turnpikes and highways and 2 mph in cities, towns, and villages in the United Kingdom. The law was initially intended to apply to steam-powered road locomotives, which were growing in popularity in England and threatening traditional railways. As cars entered the chat, drivers chafed at the restrictions. An 1896 act of Parliament brought that speed limit up to 14 mph and was thus celebrated by English motoring clubs with a 60-mile rally, an annual tradition now under the 60-mile-long name of RM Sotheby’s London to Brighton Veteran Car Run.

See all results for used cars for sale near 19805.

According to recent reports, michigan being Michigan, the day before our run brought pouring rain. It turns out vintage-car people are shockingly willing to brave weather. “I believe it rains a lot in England,” said Rick Lindner. So, we highlighted up, as did eight shining examples of the earliest entries in American motoring, from a 1904 Ford Model AC owned by Lindner to a late-model 1913 Buick Model 31 helmed by Larry and Joyce Schramm. On the Car and Driver side, we brought doughnuts, passengers, and a lot of questions about old cars.

Recent findings suggest that after the third time I asked someone for the cubic-inch displacement of their engine, John Grace (who organizes his own vintage-car run in the fall and lent his 1911 Regal to teenage brothers Jonathan and Matthew Sinclair for our tour, and whose wife, Dorothy, once drove a Model T across America, making either one of the Graces very qualified to tell me what’s what in prewar car stuff) shook his head. He told me that while he can go look it up for me, owners of cars from this era don’t generally describe their engines in displacement. “We measure in horsepower,” he mentioned. “I never hear anybody ask about cubic inches for early cars.”.

It has been revealed that it makes sense. In the modern era, cubic inches tend to reflect power output, but back in the days when a Curved Dash Oldsmobile might have a single jug measuring 95 cubic inches and making only four horsepower, it was more useful to announce your car’s 30 horsepower than, say, its 200 cubic inches.

Grace answered this, and all my other questions, with thoughtful enthusiasm, which is something I noticed about all the antique-car people I met that day.

Recent findings suggest that “The older the cars, the nicer the people,” mentioned Larry Schramm. For the hobby to have a future, he said, it needs younger people to ask questions and learn how to drive these cars. Plus, “we’re all in the same boat.” If your car isn’t the one broken on this run, it might be on the next.

Antique-car drives are a bit like off-roading; it’s best to go in pairs so someone can pick you up and get you to the finish. That happened to Ted O’Dell, when his 1913 Buick Model 31 started running a temperature. When I talked to him about it, he was unbothered. Breakdowns are just a part of the process, as they were when the cars were newly introduced. It’s historically accurate to get a flat tire.

Even though I’d invited people through different contacts, most of the participants knew one another. Many of these owners have multiple cars, maybe a significant four-door for longer tours and a Model T for local runabouts. They loan one another parts and cars and smudgy business cards for the one place that still sells horsehair upholstery stuffing.

We all gathered in a parking lot across the street from Darana Dragway. The vehicle owners hunched over crank starters to coax engines into action amid a chorus of grunts and pops, both mechanical and human. Clouds of tire smoke drifted over from the drag-strip side as smooth-bodied race machines revved big V-8s to numbers that would reduce our two- and four-cylinders to steaming puddles of Babbitt. As an example of divergent evolution, it was stark, but a show of mutual interest implied that while the bodies and power outputs were different, there was a shared soul among us.

According to recent reports, once our great eight were puffing and clattering, we left the dragsters behind in our own clouds of smoke (oil, not tire). I rode in David Liepelt’s 1915 Model T Ford at the head of the line. For Liepelt and his T, this marks a return to C/D. They were the stars of our Model T versus Model S story back in February 2014, and Liepelt is still mad that then–tech director Don Sherman beat his Ford in a Tesla, so we let him lead the tour.

Liepelt set off at a pace that would have shaken the drivers of 1896. He was all limbs, pulling the throttle lever back to full acceleration, upping the spark advance, rocking the gear-selecting pedal into high, and adjusting his Ruckstell two-speed axle. It was like watching an octopus drive a car. I had to tell him to slow down to make sure we didn’t leave anyone behind. It’s impressive what 22 horsepower is capable of, and while acceleration wasn’t going to be the challenge, nobody in the early 1900s was much for a panic stop. “Not good, but better than nothing,” Liepelt said as he barreled through an Ann Arbor intersection. If we were braking, I wasn’t aware. A line in my notebook reads, “It’s a very specific thrill to be in a car you could fall out of.”.

Thinking of joining the antiques road show? Here’s what to buy.

In a recent development, affordability was a theme among the group, which may come as a surprise to people who’ve grown up hearing terms like “Brass Era” and “prewar” only in relation to megabuck Bugattis and Duesenbergs on concours lawns. Those cars still command major prices, but more common brands have come down as older owners die and pass on to their family a garage full of acetylene headlamps and wood-spoke wheels. Our group was unanimous in suggesting a Model T as a gateway drug, including lensman James Lipman, who is now on his second T purchase (the first is shown above).

In a recent development, “The Brass Era ones may be worth $15,000 to $20,000,” mentioned T owner Brent Allen. “But you can pick up a running T for sometimes $7000, $8000 easily.” Learning to drive a Model T is a challenge, but Allen said that shouldn’t put anyone off. Other owners will be eager to teach you, and there are so many reproduction parts. If you have a frame and an engine block, you can build a whole car from catalogs.

It has been revealed that that thrill was a recurring theme. It’s the caress of wind in your hair like the first time you rode a bicycle. It’s the nervy pleasure of sitting the canter on a horse. It’s the very real possibility that you’ll never be able to stop. In a world where most cars can hit 100 mph before the end of an on-ramp, it’s amazing how exciting 35 mph can be when it takes all your extremities and maybe one or two of your passenger’s to keep the vehicle out of the nearest hedge.

According to recent reports, for Jonathan Sinclair, the youngest of our drivers at 16, learning on a vintage car ruined him for modern transportation. When he was told that he couldn’t take the driver’s test in the family Model T, his mom had to force him to do his remaining training hours in a newer car. “I don’t feel anything!” he complained. “After the involved process of driving an older car, you get in a modern car, and suddenly you don’t have to worry about anything. It feels odd.” He and his brother, Matthew, had been planning to bring their own project, a 1911 Brush, but then the Graces offered them the key to the Regal.

According to recent reports, our summer intern, Alayna Wilkening, joined the Sinclair brothers in the Regal, where she was given the job of watching the MotoMeter hood ornament for signs of overheating. Her official report was they experienced no difficulties aside from having to explain to multiple onlookers that the Regal was a Regal but not a Buick.

In a recent development, behind them, senior news editor Caleb Miller was riding in luxurious and secure comfort, cushioned in the azure-blue cabin of Daniel Coffman’s 1910 Pullman. I noticed with no small amount of jealousy that he had a nice sturdy roof support bar to hold on to in the turns. His post-run report was that his desire to purchase a vehicle of this vintage has only increased with each exposure. He also rode back with Liepelt and declared the trip “probably the most exhilarating 53 mph I’ve ever experienced.”.

Editor-in-chief Tony Quiroga was spared the terror of Liepelt’s sporty T, instead getting the full touring-car experience in Wes Raynard’s flashy red 1909 Oldsmobile Model X3, which cost about $2000 when it was new. “This is the only one known to still exist,” Raynard told me. A quick look at past auction prices highlights that the cherry Olds changed hands earlier this year for $55,105, which is considerably more than its original purchase price but a downright bargain to own a one-of-one survivor.

In a recent development, “The ride is so smooth,” Quiroga told me at our rest stop. He looked mildly disappointed that things were going so well. “I was expecting the adventure to be more adventurous. All of these enthusiasts know their cars so well that they could tear down the entire thing and rebuild it on the side of the road. Only everything is working, and we’re ahead of schedule.”.

Recent findings suggest that despite Quiroga’s desire for more chaos, the overall consensus was that the inaugural C/D London-to-Brighton (Michigan) was a great success, and the gang plans to do it again in 2027. Barring any conflicts with the steam-car rally.

Sources indicate that like a sleeper agent activated late in the game, Elana Scherr didn’t know her calling at a young age. Like many girls, she planned to be a vet-astronaut-artist, and came closest to that last one by attending UCLA art school. She painted images of cars, but did not own one. Elana reluctantly got a driver’s license at age 21 and discovered that she not only loved cars and wanted to drive them, but that other people loved cars and wanted to read about them, which meant somebody had to write about them. Since receiving activation codes, Elana has written for numerous car magazines and websites, covering classics, car culture, technology, motorsports, and latest-car reviews. In 2020, she received a Best Feature award from the Motor Press Guild for the C/D story "A Drive through Classic Americana in a Polestar 2."  In 2023, her Car and Driver feature story "In Washington, D.C.'s Secret Carpool Cabal, It's a Daily Slug Fest" was awarded 1st place in the 16th Annual National Arts & Entertainment Journalism Awards by the Los Angeles Press Club.

Industry observers note that it's been less than a week since Grand Theft Auto 6 came out, and Rockstar Games has already found another way to get us to spend money on the game. If you've been collecting sports cards while exploring Leonida, you'll soon be able to do the same outside the game. Rockstar has partnered with Panini America to bring these fictional sports trading cards to life, and they'll be out in December 2026.

This goes beyond your usual video game merchandise featuring the main characters. The cards are based on collectibles that actually exist within GTA 6's world, so you might recognize some of the athletes and teams when you open a pack. And if you're hoping to get your hands on some of the rarer cards, there are even a few that are limited to a single copy each.

Panini America declared its partnership with Rockstar Games on November 24. The officially licensed set is called the GTA VI: Sports Trading Card Collection, and it'll be the first trading card collaboration between the two companies.

It has been revealed that if you've ever collected football or basketball cards, chances are you're already familiar with Panini. They're also known for reprinting comics in Europe, and I still have a copy of the X-Men: The Last Stand Annual 2007 published by Panini Books.

Industry observers note that what's different this time is that instead of collecting cards featuring actual sports stars, you'll be collecting ones based on athletes from Rockstar's fictional universe. The promotional artwork highlights a mixture of illustrated cards and ones featuring character renders, much like those found in the game itself.

It has been revealed that the cards will come in boxes containing four packs each. Panini indicates a box will typically include two Rookie cards, a Retro card, an Illustrated card and four Special Silvers. These are average figures rather than guaranteed contents for every box.

Sources indicate that there'll also be different colored variants of the cards, including silver, pink, teal and light blue, along with team-colored parallels. The rarest variants have much smaller print runs. The Legend Bronze cards are numbered out of 49, the numbered Silver variants out of 25, and the Gold variants are one-of-a-kind cards.

Considering how many people are playing GTA 6 right now, I wouldn’t be surprised if some of the rare cards ended up selling for ridiculous prices.

Getting your hands on every variant, however, could be quite a challenge. Considering how many people are playing GTA 6 right now, I wouldn't be surprised if some of the rarer cards ended up selling for ridiculous prices.

Even if you don't care about the numbered cards, there's some appeal in having the regular ones. GTA's fictional athletes aren't exactly household names like the ones you'd find in Panini's other sports collections, but you can actually go looking for their cards in Leonida while playing the game.

According to recent reports, rockstar has been selling GTA merchandise for years, but this particular collaboration reminds me of the sort of extras that used to come with physical copies of video games. The maps that came with older GTA titles, for instance, were something you could actually use while playing and keep long after you were done with the game.

Ironically, GTA 6's boxed edition doesn't even come with a game disc. So it's nice to see Rockstar making something physical that draws directly from the game rather than simply putting its logo on another piece of merchandise.

In a recent development, rockstar could've easily gone with a conventional trading card set featuring Jason, Lucia, and other major characters. Instead, it's making replicas of things you might stumble across while taking a break from the story. I'd love to see Rockstar do something similar with other fictional brands from the series, like Sprunk or eCola.

Unfortunately, Panini hasn't unveiled an exact release date, pricing, or which countries the cards will be available in.

Depending on when the cards go on sale in December, they could make for a pretty good Christmas gift for a GTA fan.
